intro: ながら joins two things that are true of the same person at the same time. With two actions it means "while": one runs in the background while the main one, at the end of the sentence, goes ahead. With a state that clashes with what follows, the same overlap becomes "although": you are in state X and yet you do Y.

skills.rule: Verb ます-stem + ながら + main verb: one person does the main (final) action while also doing the ながら action.
skills.explain:
Take the ます-stem and add ながら: 聞きます → 聞きながら, 食べます → 食べながら, します → しながら. The action before ながら is the side activity; the verb at the end is what the sentence is about. 音楽を聞きながら勉強する is studying, with music on. Swap them and you change the focus: 勉強しながら音楽を聞く is listening to music, with some studying going on.

Both actions must have the same subject. If two different people are involved (Mum cooked while I watched TV), use 間 or 間に instead: 母が料理している間、私はテレビを見た.

The actions must last for a while. Instant verbs such as 着く, 死ぬ, 結婚する do not take ながら. It also covers long periods: 働きながら大学に通う (attend university while working). Tense and politeness go only on the final verb; ながら itself never changes.
patterns: [noun] を [verb stem] ながら [main verb]

examples.jp: 歩[ある]き{ながら}話[はな]しましょう。
音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]き{ながら}勉強[べんきょう]します。
examples.en: I study while listening to music.

examples.jp: 父[ちち]はコーヒーを飲[の]み{ながら}新聞[しんぶん]を読[よ]みます。
examples.en: My father reads the newspaper while drinking coffee.

examples.jp: スマホを見[み]{ながら}歩[ある]かないでください。
examples.en: Please don't walk while looking at your phone.

examples.jp: 兄[あに]は働[はたら]き{ながら}大学[だいがく]に通[かよ]っています。
examples.en: My older brother goes to university while working.

contrast.note: て mostly lines actions up in order: 音楽を聞いて勉強する tends to read as "listen to music, then study". ながら guarantees the two happen at the same time.
たり lists examples of things you do on different occasions (read, watch films ...), not two things done at once.
間 / 間に is "while" across two subjects: 母が寝ている間に掃除した. ながら only works when one person does both.

mistakes.bad: 食[た]べる{ながら}話[はな]します。
mistakes.good: 食[た]べ{ながら}話[はな]します。
mistakes.note: ながら follows the ます-stem (食べ), not the dictionary form.

mistakes.bad: 母[はは]が料理[りょうり]し{ながら}、私[わたし]はテレビを見[み]ました。
mistakes.good: 母[はは]が料理[りょうり]している間[あいだ]、私[わたし]はテレビを見[み]ました。
mistakes.note: Two different people: use 間, not ながら.

mistakes.bad: テレビを見[み]て{ながら}宿題[しゅくだい]をしました。
mistakes.good: テレビを見[み]{ながら}宿題[しゅくだい]をしました。
mistakes.note: Plain "while" attaches ながら straight to the stem: 見ながら, not 見てながら.

skills.tip: Ask: is it one person doing two things at once, with the last verb as the main one? Then stem + ながら.

skills.rule: X ながら(も) Y means "although X, Y": the same subject is in state X, yet Y goes against what X would lead you to expect.
skills.explain:
When the part before ながら is a state rather than an activity, ながら means "although". It attaches to a ます-stem, usually of a state such as 知っている → 知っていながら or 分かっている → 分かっていながら; to an i-adjective in its dictionary form (狭いながら); to a na-adjective or noun with nothing in between (不便ながら, 子供ながら). Adding も (ながらも) makes the contrast stronger; the meaning is the same.

The subject of both halves is the same, and the tone is fairly formal or written. A few set phrases are everyday Japanese: 残念ながら (unfortunately), 失礼ながら (if I may say so), 小さいながらも (small as it is).

With an action verb, ながら normally means "while". It reads as "although" only when the two halves clearly clash: 悪いと知りながら嘘をついた.
patterns: [verb stem, often ～てい] ながら(も)
残念ながら / 失礼ながら

examples.jp: 残念[ざんねん]{ながら}、今回[こんかい]は参加[さんか]できません。
examples.en: Unfortunately, I can't take part this time.

examples.jp: この部屋[へや]は狭[せま]い{ながらも}、明[あか]るくて快適[かいてき]です。
examples.en: Although this room is small, it's bright and comfortable.

examples.jp: 小[ちい]さい{ながらも}、自分[じぶん]の店[みせ]を持[も]つことができました。
examples.en: It's only a small one, but I managed to get a shop of my own.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は本当[ほんとう]のことを知[し]ってい{ながら}、何[なに]も言[い]わなかった。
examples.en: Although he knew the truth, he said nothing.

examples.jp: 体[からだ]に悪[わる]いと分[わ]かってい{ながら}、つい食[た]べてしまう。
examples.en: Even though I know it's bad for me, I end up eating it anyway.

contrast.note: のに is the everyday "even though", often with surprise or complaint, and allows two subjects: 雨が降っているのに、弟は出かけた. ながら(も) needs one subject and sounds more formal and matter-of-fact.
けど / が is a neutral "but" for any two clauses in conversation. ながら(も) is tighter: one subject, one state, one contrary result.
つつ(も) is a more literary twin that attaches only to verbs: 知りつつも. ながら(も) also takes adjectives and nouns.

mistakes.bad: この町[まち]は不便[ふべん]な{ながらも}、住[す]みやすいです。
mistakes.good: この町[まち]は不便[ふべん]{ながらも}、住[す]みやすいです。
mistakes.note: Na-adjectives and nouns attach to ながら directly, with no な or の.

mistakes.bad: 危[あぶ]ないと分[わ]かっていた{ながら}、止[と]めなかった。
mistakes.good: 危[あぶ]ないと分[わ]かってい{ながら}、止[と]めなかった。
mistakes.note: ながら never takes tense: it follows the stem (分かってい), and the final verb carries the past.

skills.tip: State or adjective before ながら, and a "yet" after it: that is "although". Two activities at once: that is "while".
